title: Can, must, want, may
goal: Master the five Dutch modal verbs and dodge their biggest trap: *moet niet*, which does not mean "don't have to".
bekal: using *kunnen, moeten, mogen, willen, zullen* correctly
sending the main verb to the end of the sentence
telling *je hoeft niet* (you don't have to) from *je moet niet* (you mustn't)
wave: Go back to **unit 11**: picture the route from your home to the nearest station, then describe all of it in Dutch, sentence by sentence.

dialogs.title: Dialog — Verhuizen
dialogs.intro: Budi is moving rooms. He needs help, and the Dutch turn moving day into a group effort: *een verhuizing*.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sanne, kun je me zaterdag helpen?
lines.id: Sanne, can you help me on Saturday?
lines.literal: Sanne, can you me Saturday help?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik moet verhuizen. Ik mag mijn kamer niet houden.
lines.id: I have to move. I can't keep my room.
lines.literal: I must move. I may my room not keep.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: When do you have to be out?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Voor het einde van de maand. Ik kan een busje huren.
lines.id: Before the end of the month. I can rent a van.
lines.literal: before the end of the month. I can a little-bus rent.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Dat hoeft niet. Mijn broer heeft een bakfiets.
lines.id: No need. My brother has a cargo bike.
lines.literal: that need not. my brother has a box-bike.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Een bakfiets? Voor een hele kamer?
lines.id: A cargo bike? For a whole room?
lines.literal: a box-bike? for a whole room?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Je zou verbaasd zijn. Alles past erin.
lines.literal: you would surprised be. everything fits in-it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Goed. Maar we moeten niet in de regen rijden.
lines.id: Okay. But we mustn't ride in the rain.
lines.literal: good. but we must not in the rain ride.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Dat kunnen we niet beloven. Zullen we om negen uur beginnen?
lines.id: We can't promise that. Shall we start at nine?
lines.literal: that can we not promise. shall we at nine hour begin?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Prima. Ik zal koffie en broodjes halen.
lines.id: Great. I'll get coffee and rolls.
lines.literal: fine. I shall coffee and rolls fetch.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Dan wil iedereen wel komen helpen.
lines.id: Then everyone will want to come and help.
lines.literal: then wants everyone indeed come help.

notes: **Kun je me helpen?** — *kunt* shortens to *kun* only before *je*. Both are correct; *kun je* is far more common.
**Wat moet er gebeuren?** — notice the main verb (*gebeuren*) standing at the end in its dictionary form. This pattern holds for every modal verb.
**Ik mag mijn kamer niet houden** — *mogen* means "may, be allowed", and *mag niet* means "not allowed" (forbidden), not just "can't".

**Dat hoeft niet.** Here is the pair you must never swap: *moeten niet* = **mustn't** (a prohibition), while *hoeven niet* = **don't have to**. The verb *hoeven* is practically only used in the negative.

**Een bakfiets** — a bike with a big box in front, which the Dutch use to carry kids, groceries, furniture, and yes, an entire student room. It's one of the most typically Dutch objects of modern times.
**Je zou verbaasd zijn** — *zou* is the conditional of *zullen*: "you would be surprised". It's also the key to advanced politeness (*zou u … kunnen?*).
**Zullen we om negen uur beginnen?** — *zullen we …?* is the standard way to suggest something: "shall we …?". Almost every invitation in Dutch starts like this.

**Dan wil iedereen wel komen helpen** — two verbs lined up at the end (*komen helpen*). Dutch lets the verb pile at the end grow to three or four; that's what gives its long sentences their distinctive sound.

grammars.title: The five modal verbs
body: All of them put the main verb **at the end of the sentence in its dictionary form**, and all are slightly irregular in the singular.
after: Note that the *jij* form here has **no** -t for *moeten* and *mogen* — that's simply the form, not inversion.
Word order: subject → modal (position 2) → the rest → **main verb at the end**. *Ik **kan** morgen niet **komen**.*
Separable verbs (unit 9) join up again at the end: *Ik moet vroeg **opstaan**.*

grammars.title: Shades that change the meaning
body: The five can look alike in translation, yet they are far apart.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: I can't come (something's in the way).

after: ⚠️ Rows five and six are the heart of this unit. Answering an invitation with *ik moet niet komen* means "I mustn't come" — not "I don't have to come". English *must not* works the same way, so let it guide you.
*Hoeven* always takes **te** before its main verb: *Je hoeft niet **te** betalen.* It's the only one in this group that does.
*Kunnen* is also used for speaking a language: *Ik kan Nederlands* — with no second verb at all.

head: Nederlands
Politeness level
rows: careful, when it may be a bother

blocks.text: The word *even* is the most useful softener in Dutch: it shrinks a request to "just for a moment". *Kun je even kijken?*, *Mag ik even bellen?*, *Wacht even.* Without *even*, the same request sounds much more demanding.

blocks.title: Answering a request
items: *Ik zal kijken wat ik kan doen* — I'll see what I can do.
*Sorry, dat lukt me niet* — sorry, I can't manage that. (*lukken* = to succeed, work out)
*Misschien een andere keer* — maybe another time.

head: Nederlands
English
rows: Je moet je fiets op slot zetten.
You have to lock your bike.
Je hoeft geen afspraak te maken.
I still have to do the shopping.
Dat mag niet van mijn baas.

blocks.text: *Op slot zetten* (to lock) is worth learning whole: in the Netherlands, bikes are locked twice — one lock on the wheel, one chain to a post. That's not paranoia; hundreds of thousands of bikes go missing every year.
*Boodschappen doen* = doing the grocery shopping, as opposed to *winkelen* (going around the shops for clothes and things). English makes the same split: "doing the shopping" versus "going shopping".
